Greater Manchester Police officers were called to the incident on South Street in Lower Openshaw, Manchester, at about 12:50 BST. title: Body building products seized in raids in Rochdale and Manchester

input.lead: Up to a million tablets were confiscated during the raids on a suspects organised crime group
input.summary: Up to a million tablets were confiscated during the raids on a suspects organised crime group
input.evidence_text: Body building products seized in raids in Rochdale and Manchester - BBC News Image source, Greater Manchester Police Image caption, Police raids took place at a suspected drug safe house off Manchester Road in Rochdale By Richard Stead and Naj Modak , North West Published 28 September 2026 Four people have been arrested after police seized what they believe could be up to one million illicit pharmaceutical drugs during raids linked to an organised crime group. Three arrests were made at four addresses in Rochdale following a six-month investigation. A fourth person was arrested in Manchester. Officers suspect the group was distributing drugs including diazepam, bodybuilding products and weight-loss medications across the UK. Det Insp Rich McCorry said there were "serious dangers" associated with unlicensed drugs being sold to the public. Image caption, Det Insp Rich McCorry said officers executed six warrants on Thursday Two men aged 23 and 52 were arrested at an address on Twingate in Rochdale. A 51-year-old man was arrested on Whittaker Lane in the town, while a 44-year-old man was arrested on Kingsway in Manchester. All four were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to supply Class A, B and C drugs and remain in custody. Police said they believe up to one million tablets were recovered during the operation, which targeted properties linked to suspected drug storage and distribution. Greater Manchester Police executed six warrants as part of a six-month investigation led by its Serious Organised Crime Group. McCorry said officers used surveillance, drug seizures, phone analysis and automatic number plate recognition data to build evidence against the suspects. title: Cellist 'emotional' at being able to play again after major crash injury

input.lead: Cellist Clara Simpson was left with long-term injuries in a crash on her way to work
input.summary: Cellist Clara Simpson was left with long-term injuries in a crash on her way to work
input.evidence_text: A musician who was seriously injured in a crash has said that being able to play her instrument again for just a few minutes felt like "getting part of herself back" Clara Hope Simpson was traveling from Manchester to Sheffield for her first day in a teaching role at Sheffield Music Academy when the car in which she was a passenger hit a large patch of ice and flipped onto its roof The incident, on A57 Snake Pass on 1 March, 2025, left the then 26-year-old in hospital for ten days with two fractured vertebrae The 28-year-old said: "It was the most terrifying experience of my life. Originally from Toronto in Canada, Clara moved to Manchester in 2021 to complete her postgraduate studies, and has since worked as a freelance classical cellist, touring and performing internationally Following the crash, she developed a condition which weakened one of her vocal cords after surgery through the front of her neck to treat her spine

input.evidence_text: Every morning at 11 almost exactly on the dot, a group of men gather on the ground floor of the Northern Quarter Car Park: that tall, graffiti-coated building on the corner of Church and Tib Street One by one they unlock the padlocks dangling from the back of their flat-tyred vans, and the doors swing open. Out from within comes cart after cart full of corn This is the not-entirely-secret HQ of the Market Street corn vendors: a four-storey council-owned car park, sitting across two of Manchester’s busiest streets. When I get there, the men are working in silence, hands sheathed in black gloves, bags of sweetcorn torn open, cardboard Just as I’m about to approach a vendor, I’m forwarded an email from a reader. It has the subject line The Mystery We All Want Solved "The reason I’m writing is because the people of Manchester are desperate to know what the hell is going on with all of the corn sellers on Market St "Why are there now so many of them? How on earth do they make a profit? Are they independent vendors or all part of the same company? Is their presence legal? What does their proliferation say about the state of the city centre?”

The plans attracted objections from 10 neighbouring households and were called in for consideration by Trafford's Planning and Development Management Committee by a local councillor over parking and highways concerns. title: Is the funding market getting harder and what could that mean for Manchester? | Manchester Digital

input.lead: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing.
input.summary: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised
input.evidence_text: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised. More capital is being concentrated in fewer companies while the market for exits remains difficult Financial news recently added another dimension to that discussion. AI-related shares fell last week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower approach to the development of increasingly capable AI models. Nvidia finished the day down 3.4%, SoftBank fell 10.7% in Tokyo Additionally, the Bank of England is predicted to increase interest rates later this year, which could affect the North West's tech funding landscape by raising the cost of capital across the board, compressing valuations, pushing investors toward profitability over growth-at-all The British Business Bank's 2026 Small Business Equity Tracker found that equity investment into UK smaller businesses fell 4% to £12.3bn in 2025. Seed deal numbers fell 27% and venture deals fell 13%. AI companies attracted 44% of all investment into smaller businesses while the Beauhurst recorded £14.4bn of UK equity investment across 2,799 deals in the first half of 2026 but three AI companies accounted for 29% of all the capital raised. Those very large rounds can make the overall market look stronger than it feels to businesses raising at seed or Ser Beauhurst's analysis shows that UK equity investment more than doubled between 2017 and 2021 to £32.2bn while annual exits remained at around 400 to 500. An exit takes a median of four years from a funding round
